title: Everyday Customs in France and the USA: Social Greetings
summary: First, we look at greetings and how they show closeness. Next, we look at French words that create polite distance, and at American small talk with strangers.

cover.alt: A woman greets a French baker while a man leaves a tip for an American diner server.

blocks.title: Introduction
paragraphs: First, we look at greetings and how they show closeness. Next, we look at French words that create polite distance, and at American small talk with strangers. Then we explain why tipping matters so much in the USA. Last, we compare French and American meals.

items.prompt: How do you greet a good friend, and how do you greet a new person at work?
Do you talk to strangers in a shop or on a bus? Why or why not?
Have you ever felt that someone stood too close to you?

blocks.title: Part 1: A Greeting Measures the Relationship
paragraphs: Picture two meetings. In Marseille, two old friends kiss on both cheeks. In Chicago, two people meet and choose a handshake or a hug. Earlier, we saw that the relationship chooses the greeting. Here, we look at what happens when the greeting is missing, and at how body space works.

A cheek kiss is an informal greeting. It can show friendship, family ties, respect or comfort. So in places where cheek kissing is normal, the kiss carries a message. If you do *not* kiss, people may read a message too. They can feel dislike or offense.

France is not the same everywhere. The number of kisses changes from region to region. There is even a French joke: you can know which city you are in by counting the kisses. In southern France, even two men often greet with cheek kisses. In northern France, this happens less. So "the French kiss" is really many local habits.

What about handshakes and hugs? In some English-speaking countries, such as Australia and New Zealand, cheek kisses happen only among close friends, and handshakes or hugs are more common greetings. A handshake or a hug can do the same job as a kiss: it says how close two people are, but with a different kind of touch.

Body space also has rules. Scientists who study space between people describe four zones: intimate, personal, social and public. We let a person into a closer zone when we feel closer to them. Americans like about the same personal space as people in northern and central Europe. In Japan, everyday greetings usually have less touching, so kisses, hugs and handshakes are less common than in many other places.
So a greeting is like a ruler. It measures the relationship, and each culture marks the lines in a slightly different place.

images.alt: Friends share a cheek greeting on a French street; two acquaintances shake hands on an American sidewalk.

blocks.title: Check: Part 1: A Greeting Measures the Relationship

items.prompt: Why can it seem unfriendly not to kiss someone in a culture where cheek kissing is normal?
items.answer: Because the kiss is a sign of friendship, respect or family ties. When people expect it and it does not happen, they can read that as dislike or offense.
items.explanation: Where would you put a cheek kiss among the four zones: intimate, personal, social or public?

blocks.title: Part 2: French Words That Build Polite Distance
paragraphs: In France, you enter a bakery and say, "A baguette, please." The baker looks less friendly than before. What went wrong? You forgot one word: *Bonjour*.

Saying *Bonjour* before any request is a basic rule of politeness in shops, cafés and bakeries. It helps you avoid a cold welcome. People appreciate it even if it is the only French word you know. The word comes first because it treats the worker as a person first and a service second.

The French words *tu* and *vous* do a similar job. Both mean "you." *Tu* is close and informal. *Vous* shows respect or social distance. Many languages have a choice like this. In the past, French speakers often used *tu* and *vous* in the same situations. Over time, clearer patterns grew. English *you* is different. It is less formal than *vous*, and it does not push people apart.
This matters for visitors. When a French person uses *vous* with you, it is not coldness. It is respect. Distance at the start is a polite way to say, "I take you seriously."

blocks.title: Check: Part 2: French Words That Build Polite Distance

items.prompt: Why does a French shop worker expect "Bonjour" before a request?
items.answer: Because it is a basic politeness rule. It greets the worker as a person before you ask for a service, and it helps avoid an unwelcoming situation.
items.explanation: Does your language have a polite "you" and a close "you"? When do you change from one to the other?

blocks.title: Part 3: American Small Talk Opens and Closes Doors
paragraphs: In a line at an American supermarket, a stranger says, "Cold today, huh?" You may never see this person again. So why talk at all?

Small talk opens a conversation. It shows strangers that you have friendly plans, not bad ones. It also keeps social bonds alive and helps people manage the distance between them. Small talk works at the end of a talk too. A few light words like "Have a good day!" make leaving softer, so it does not feel like rejection.

So small talk is a tool for the edges of a relationship. It lets two strangers be warm for one minute and then leave without any problem. This is why some visitors misunderstand Americans. They hear friendly words and expect a deep friendship. But the friendly words are often a polite way to share a small, safe space.
Compare this with France. French politeness puts the respectful word, *Bonjour*, at the door. American politeness often puts a light chat there. Both are careful ways to handle a stranger.

images.alt: Two strangers chat at a bus stop, then wave as they part.

blocks.title: Check: Part 3: American Small Talk Opens and Closes Doors

items.prompt: What two jobs can small talk do at the start and at the end of a conversation?
items.answer: At the start, it opens the talk and shows friendly plans. At the end, it makes leaving softer, so the other person does not feel rejected.
items.explanation: Is small talk with strangers friendly, false or something in between? Explain your choice.

blocks.title: Part 4: Why American Workers Count on Tips
paragraphs: An American visitor in Paris leaves a big tip that nobody expected. A French visitor in New York leaves no tip, and the server is upset. Both made the same mistake from opposite sides.

History helps explain this. In 1919, Prohibition put money pressure on restaurants in the USA. So they accepted tips to add to their workers' pay. In this way, the tip slowly became part of the wage, not only a small extra "thank you." That is why many American workers depend on tips.

But the system has problems. Tipping can feel awkward, because people are not sure how much to give. It is also not always fair. People sometimes tip by the price of the meal, not by the quality of the service. And the system is hard to change. Some people argue that changing the tip rules could favor servers who get tips over staff who do not get tips, and make income less equal.
So in the USA, a tip is not a gift you can easily skip. It is part of how workers get paid.

blocks.title: Check: Part 4: Why American Workers Count on Tips

items.prompt: How did Prohibition in 1919 help make tipping part of workers' pay in the USA?
items.answer: Prohibition put money pressure on restaurants. They accepted tips to add to workers' wages, so tips became part of the pay.
items.explanation: Should a tip reward good service, or should it simply be part of the price? Why?

blocks.title: Part 5: What a Meal Protects
paragraphs: At lunchtime in Paris, office workers leave their desks to eat. In many American towns, lunch may be a quick burger. Is one way better? It is more useful to ask what each meal protects.

In France, enjoying food is an important value. In the 20th century, Georges Auguste Escoffier wrote down the rules of high French cooking. Today, a lunch break usually lasts at least one hour. Eating lunch at your desk is even illegal. But a long lunch does not mean a big meal. On busy workdays in Paris, lunches with many courses are not common. French food has also changed. Many modern meals are simpler, and some dishes come from immigrant cooking. Fast food and new habits among young people put pressure on the old food culture. Even so, France works to keep it, for example through education programs in schools.

American food grew from a different story. US culture was shaped by history, geography and immigration. Famous foods like apple pie and hamburgers come from immigrant and local roots. Fast food is a common part of American meals, and people worry that it adds calories and leads to health problems.
So the French lunch protects time to enjoy food with others. The quick American meal reflects a mixed food story and a busy day.

images.alt: Adults share a relaxed French lunch while a worker eats a quick sandwich lunch beside an American office.

blocks.title: Check: Part 5: What a Meal Protects

items.prompt: Does a long French lunch break mean a big meal with many courses every workday?
items.answer: No. Lunch breaks usually last at least one hour, but lunches with many courses are not common on workdays in busy cities like Paris.
items.explanation: What does your usual lunch protect: time, money, health or company?

blocks.title: Final Reflection
blocks.intro: At the start, it was easy to think that Americans are friendly and the French are cold. Now we can see that both cultures are careful about closeness, but they place warmth in different moments. The French show respect first with *Bonjour*, *vous* and a slow lunch, while Americans show warmth quickly with small talk, and they also pay workers through tips.

items.prompt: Which custom from France or the USA would be hardest for you to follow, and why?
Think of one custom in your country. What does it say about closeness or distance between people?
